lessons.title: Chromatography
lessons.focus: principles of separation, thin-layer and gas chromatography

data.title: Chromatography
data.summary: This lesson explains how chromatography separates mixtures based on different interactions with a stationary phase and a mobile phase, focusing on thin‑layer chromatography (TLC) and gas chromatography (GC). Students will learn the key concepts, equipment, and practical steps for each technique.
objectives: Describe the basic principle of separation in chromatography
Identify the components of a TLC system and explain how a sample moves
Interpret a TLC plate to determine relative polarity of compounds
Outline the main parts of a gas chromatograph and the role of the carrier gas
Explain how retention time is used to identify substances in GC
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand basic concepts of mixtures, solubility, and the idea of a stationary versus a mobile phase from earlier lessons on sampling and preparation.
why: Chromatography is used every day, from testing food safety to detecting pollutants in water, because it can separate tiny amounts of chemicals that look identical to the naked eye.
In industry, TLC helps chemists quickly check the purity of a drug, while GC is essential for monitoring air quality, ensuring that harmful gases are detected and controlled.

sections.heading: What is Chromatography?
sections.body:
Chromatography is a laboratory technique that lets us pull apart the different substances hidden inside a mixture. Imagine you have a bag of mixed coloured candies – red, blue, green, and yellow – and you want to separate each colour without opening every single wrapper. In chromatography we do something similar, but with invisible molecules instead of candies.  

The basic idea is that the mixture is moved through a material that holds onto some parts of the mixture more strongly than others. The material that does the holding is called the **stationary phase** – “stationary” means it stays in one place. The liquid or gas that carries the mixture along is called the **mobile phase** – “mobile” means it moves. As the mobile phase travels, each component of the mixture interacts differently with the stationary phase. Those that stick more tightly move slowly, while those that stick less move quickly. After a certain distance, the components become separated into distinct zones that we can see or detect.

> **Definition:** *Chromatography* is a method of separating the individual components of a mixture by passing it through a stationary phase while a mobile phase moves it along.

Why does this work? Molecules have different physical and chemical properties – such as size, polarity, or ability to dissolve in a solvent. When a molecule meets the stationary phase, forces like attraction, adsorption, or solubility determine how long it stays attached. The mobile phase continuously pushes the mixture forward, so each molecule spends a different amount of time “stuck” versus “traveling.” This difference creates a separation.

> **Note:** The separation power of chromatography depends on choosing a stationary phase and a mobile phase that interact differently with the substances you want to separate.

A simple everyday comparison is a marathon race on a sticky track. All runners start together, but some wear shoes that grip the track more than others. The runners with less grip slide forward faster, while the ones with sticky shoes lag behind. After a while, the runners are spread out along the track according to how much they were slowed down. In chromatography the runners are the molecules, the sticky track is the stationary phase, and the wind that pushes them forward is the mobile phase.

To see the concept in action, picture a strip of paper (the stationary phase) dipped briefly into a drop of ink mixed with water (the mobile phase). As the water climbs up the paper by capillary action, the different colour pigments in the ink travel at different speeds. After a few minutes, you can see separate coloured spots – each spot represents a different pigment that has been separated.

Mathematically, the distance a component travels is often expressed as the **retention factor** $R_f$:

$$
R_f = \frac{\text{distance travelled by the component}}{\text{distance travelled by the solvent front}}
$$

The $R_f$ value is a simple number between 0 and 1 that tells us how strongly a component interacted with the stationary phase. A small $R_f$ (close to 0) means the component stayed near the start – it liked the stationary phase. A large $R_f$ (close to 1) means it moved almost as far as the solvent front – it preferred the mobile phase.

> **In daily life:** Chromatography is used to test the purity of medicines, to detect pollutants in water, and even to separate the flavors that make coffee taste different.

Because the principle is so general, many versions of chromatography exist – thin‑layer chromatography (TLC) uses a flat plate, gas chromatography (GC) uses a gas as the mobile phase, and liquid chromatography (LC) uses a liquid. All of them rely on the same core idea: a stationary phase that stays put, a mobile phase that moves, and different interactions that cause the mixture’s components to spread out.

> **Remember:** The key to successful chromatography is matching the right stationary phase with the right mobile phase so that the substances you care about separate cleanly.

sections.heading: Key Terms: Stationary Phase, Mobile Phase, Retention
sections.body:
When we talk about chromatography we are really describing a race. Imagine a long hallway where many runners start together, but each runner is slowed down by a different kind of carpet on the floor. Some runners glide easily, while others get stuck a little on the carpet fibers. In chromatography the “runners” are the individual molecules of a mixture, the “hallway” is the column or plate, and the “carpets” are the two phases that the molecules interact with.

**Stationary phase** is the part of the system that stays put – it does not move with the flow of the sample. It can be a thin layer of silica gel on a glass plate (as in TLC) or a packed column of tiny beads inside a tube (as in GC or liquid chromatography). The surface of the stationary phase is covered with chemical groups that can attract or repel different molecules. Because it is fixed, any molecule that sticks to it for a moment will be delayed while the mobile phase carries the rest forward.

**Mobile phase** is the fluid that moves through the stationary phase, carrying the sample along. In thin‑layer chromatography the mobile phase is a liquid solvent that climbs up the plate by capillary action. In gas chromatography the mobile phase is an inert gas such as helium or nitrogen that is pushed through the column by a pump. The mobile phase can be thought of as the “wind” that pushes the runners down the hallway.

**Retention** describes how long a molecule stays attached to the stationary phase before it continues moving with the mobile phase. The longer the retention, the slower the molecule travels through the system. Retention is usually expressed as a time (retention time) or as a distance (how far the spot moves on a TLC plate). Mathematically, the retention factor $R_f$ for TLC is defined as  

$$
R_f = \frac{\text{distance traveled by the compound}}{\text{distance traveled by the solvent front}}
$$  

A small $R_f$ (close to 0) means the compound sticks strongly to the stationary phase and moves only a short way; a large $R_f$ (close to 1) means it hardly interacts with the stationary phase and rides quickly with the mobile phase.

> **Definition:** *Stationary phase* – the fixed material that interacts with sample molecules and slows them down.  
> **Definition:** *Mobile phase* – the moving liquid or gas that transports the sample through the stationary phase.  
> **Definition:** *Retention* – the degree to which a molecule is held back by the stationary phase, measured as time or distance.

Why do different molecules travel at different speeds? The answer lies in the types of forces that can act between a molecule and each phase. Common interactions include:

* **Polarity** – polar molecules (those with uneven charge distribution) are attracted to polar stationary phases, while non‑polar molecules prefer a non‑polar stationary phase.  
* **Hydrogen bonding** – molecules that can donate or accept hydrogen bonds may stick to a stationary phase that contains –OH or –NH groups.  
* **Size and shape** – larger molecules may fit poorly into the pores of a packed column and therefore move more slowly.

Consider a simple everyday comparison: think of a sponge soaked with water (the stationary phase) and a stream of air blowing over it (the mobile phase). If you drop a tiny oil droplet onto the sponge, it will cling to the water‑filled pores and be carried away slowly. A drop of alcohol, which mixes well with water, will spread quickly and be swept away faster by the air. The same principle works in chromatography: the chemical “affinity” between a molecule and the stationary phase decides how long it is retained.

> **In daily life:** The way a coffee filter holds back coffee grounds while letting liquid pass is a macroscopic example of a stationary phase (the filter paper) and a mobile phase (the water‑based coffee).

A common source of confusion is to think that the mobile phase “pushes” molecules because it is stronger. In reality, the mobile phase simply provides a pathway; the real control over speed comes from how strongly each molecule is attracted to the stationary phase.  

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that a faster‑moving solvent always makes all components separate quicker. If the stationary phase is too weakly interacting, the components may all travel together and give no separation.

> **Remember:** The key to successful chromatography is choosing a stationary phase and a mobile phase whose interactions differ enough for the components you want to separate. By adjusting polarity, temperature, or solvent composition, you can fine‑tune the retention of each molecule and turn a chaotic mixture into a clear, ordered pattern.

sections.heading: Thin‑Layer Chromatography (TLC) Basics
sections.body:
Imagine you have a tiny, flat “road map” that can separate the different ingredients in a mixture, much like a kitchen sieve separates flour from sugar. That map is the **thin‑layer chromatography (TLC) plate**, and it works by letting the mixture travel across a thin layer of material while the components split apart based on how they like the surface versus the surrounding liquid.

**What the TLC plate looks like**  
A TLC plate is a small rectangle of glass, plastic, or aluminum foil that is coated with a very thin layer of an adsorbent material, most often silica gel (tiny glass‑like particles). The coating is called the **stationary phase** because it stays in one place while the liquid moves over it. The surface is usually white or slightly off‑white, and the coating is so thin you can barely see it without a microscope.

**Preparing the plate – spotting the sample**  
1. **Draw a faint line** about 1 cm from the bottom edge of the plate with a pencil. This line is called the **origin line**; it tells you where to place the sample.  
2. Using a clean capillary tube (a thin glass tube) or a tiny pipette, **place a small drop** of the solution you want to test onto the origin line. The drop should be no larger than a grain of sand; a tiny dot is enough.  
3. Let the spot **dry completely** before you move the plate. If the solvent evaporates, the sample stays fixed at the origin and will not smear when the plate is developed.

> **Note:** *Always use a fresh capillary for each different sample to avoid cross‑contamination.*

**Developing the plate – letting the mobile phase move**  
The **mobile phase** is a liquid (or mixture of liquids) that travels up the plate by capillary action, carrying the sample with it. Common mobile phases are mixtures like hexane‑ethyl acetate or chloroform‑methanol, chosen to give the right balance of polarity for the substances you are testing.

1. **Prepare a developing chamber** – a glass jar with a lid works well. Pour a small amount of the mobile phase into the bottom so that the liquid level is **below** the origin line (usually 0.5 cm).  
2. **Place a piece of filter paper** inside the jar, touching the wall. This paper helps keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapor, which makes the solvent front rise evenly.  
3. **Put the TLC plate into the chamber** without letting the origin line touch the liquid. Close the lid tightly.  
4. As the solvent climbs, it carries each component of the mixture upward. Some components stick more strongly to the silica (they are “polar”) and move slowly; others prefer the solvent (they are “non‑polar”) and rush ahead.

When the solvent front reaches about 1 cm from the top of the plate, **remove the plate** and immediately mark the solvent front with a pencil (this line is called the **Rf line**). Then let the plate **dry** in a fume hood or a safe area.

**Visualizing the spots – seeing what was hidden**  
Many compounds are invisible to the naked eye. To make the spots appear, you can use one of several methods:

* **UV light:** If the TLC plate was made with a fluorescent indicator, shining a UV lamp (usually 254 nm) will cause many organic compounds to glow as dark spots against a bright background.  
* **Staining reagents:** Spraying the plate with a chemical like iodine vapor, ninhydrin (for amino acids), or a phosphomolybdic acid solution will produce colored spots after a short heating step.  
* **Heat:** Some reagents develop color only after the plate is gently heated with a hair dryer or a hot plate.

**Calculating the retention factor (Rf)**  
For each visible spot, you can calculate how far it traveled relative to the solvent front:

$$
Rf = \frac{\text{distance from origin to spot}}{\text{distance from origin to solvent front}}
$$

The $Rf$ value is always between 0 and 1 and is characteristic for a given compound under specific conditions. By comparing $Rf$ values with those of known standards, you can **identify** unknown substances.

> **Definition:** *Retention factor (Rf) – a simple ratio that tells how far a compound moved on the TLC plate relative to the solvent front.*

**Why TLC is useful**  
TLC is quick, inexpensive, and requires only a tiny amount of sample (often less than a milligram). It lets you check the purity of a reaction mixture, monitor the progress of a synthesis, or decide which solvent system will work best for a larger‑scale chromatography.

> **In daily life:** *Think of TLC like a fingerprint test at a crime scene. Just as a unique pattern can identify a person, a unique set of $Rf$ values can identify a chemical.*

**Common pitfalls to avoid**  
If the spot is too large, the components will overlap and you won’t get clear separation. Also, never let the origin line sit in the solvent; the sample would dissolve away and give no spots at all.

> **Remember:** *Keep the sample spot small, let it dry completely, and choose a mobile phase that gives a good spread of $Rf$ values (some near 0.2, others near 0.8) for the best separation.*

sections.heading: Interpreting TLC Results
sections.body:
When you look at a TLC plate after it has been developed, the first thing you see are a series of coloured spots.  
Each spot is a different compound that has moved up the plate with the solvent (the **mobile phase**).  
The distance each spot travels tells you how strongly that compound interacts with the **stationary phase** (the thin layer of silica or alumina that coats the plate).  

> **Definition:** *Retention factor* (written **Rf**) is a simple number that compares how far a compound moved to how far the solvent front moved.

Why do we need a number?  
Imagine you are comparing the speed of two cars on a race track that has a different length each time you race.  
If you only said “Car A went 30 m and Car B went 20 m”, the result would be confusing because the track length might have been 100 m one day and 50 m another day.  
Instead, you would say “Car A covered 30 % of the track, Car B covered 20 % of the track”.  
The percentage removes the dependence on the track length and lets you compare the cars directly.  
Rf does exactly the same thing for TLC spots: it removes the dependence on how far the solvent actually traveled in that particular run.

### Step‑by‑step calculation of Rf

1. **Mark the start line.**  
   This is the line where you originally spotted your sample, usually near the bottom of the plate. Call this point *origin*.

2. **Find the solvent front.**  
   After the plate dries, draw a faint line at the highest point reached by the solvent. This is the *solvent front*.

3. **Measure distances.**  
   - Use a ruler or a piece of paper to measure the distance from the origin to the centre of the spot you are interested in. Call this distance *d₁*.  
   - Measure the distance from the origin to the solvent front. Call this distance *d₂*.

4. **Apply the formula.**  

   $$\text{Rf} = \frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}$$

   Because both distances are measured in the same units (millimetres or centimetres), the units cancel and you obtain a pure number between 0 and 1.

5. **Record the value.**  
   Write the Rf next to the spot on your plate sketch. Do this for every spot you see.

### Using Rf to compare polarity

Silica gel, the most common stationary phase, is **polar** – it likes to hold onto polar molecules.  
The mobile phase (usually a mixture of non‑polar and polar solvents) is less polar.  

- **Polar compounds** interact strongly with the silica, so they travel only a short distance. Their Rf values are low (close to 0).  
- **Non‑polar compounds** do not stick to the silica and are carried further by the solvent. Their Rf values are high (close to 1).

> **In daily life:** Think of a sticky note on a smooth table. If the note is very sticky (polar), it will stay near where you placed it. If it is only slightly sticky (non‑polar), it will slide farther when you push the table gently.

### Practical tips for reliable Rf values

- **Use the same solvent mixture** each time you run a plate. Changing the proportion of, say, hexane and ethyl acetate will change how far every spot moves, and the Rf values will no longer be comparable.  
- **Measure from the centre of the spot**, not from its edge, because spots can spread unevenly.  
- **Run a reference compound** with a known Rf on the same plate. This gives you a built‑in check that your measurements are correct.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to draw the solvent‑front line before the solvent evaporates. If the line is missing, you cannot determine *d₂* and the Rf calculation becomes impossible.

### Quick checklist

- Origin marked → ✔  
- Solvent front marked → ✔  
- Distances measured from origin → ✔  
- Rf calculated with the formula → ✔  
- Compare Rf values to infer polarity → ✔  

By following these steps, you turn a colourful pattern on a TLC plate into quantitative data that tells you how polar each component is, and you can compare unknown samples to known standards with confidence.

sections.heading: Gas Chromatography (GC) Overview
sections.body:
Gas chromatography (GC) is a technique that separates tiny amounts of chemicals that are already in the gas phase.  
Think of it as a race track for molecules: each molecule enters the track, moves along a long, narrow tube, and finishes at a different time depending on how fast it can travel. By watching when each molecule reaches the finish line, we can identify and measure it.

### Main parts of a GC instrument  

1. **Carrier gas** – This is the “air” that pushes the sample through the system. It is an inert (non‑reactive) gas such as helium, nitrogen, or hydrogen. Because it does not react with the sample, it simply carries the molecules along the column, much like a conveyor belt moves packages without changing them.

2. **Injection port** – The place where a tiny drop of liquid or a small amount of gas is introduced. The port quickly heats the sample so that it vaporises and mixes with the carrier gas.

3. **Column** – A very thin, usually coiled tube (often 30 m long but only 0.25 mm wide) that is packed with a stationary phase or coated on the inside with a thin film. The stationary phase is a material that interacts slightly with the sample molecules. As the carrier gas pushes the vapor through, each molecule spends a little time “sticking” to the stationary phase and a little time moving with the gas. Molecules that interact strongly stay longer; those that interact weakly zip through faster. This difference creates the separation.

4. **Oven** – The column sits inside a temperature‑controlled oven. By heating the oven, we can change how strongly the stationary phase holds onto the molecules. Raising the temperature makes all molecules move faster, which is useful for separating compounds that would otherwise stick too long.

5. **Detector** – At the end of the column, the detector watches the exiting molecules and turns their arrival into an electrical signal. Common detectors include the flame ionisation detector (FID) and the thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The detector’s output is plotted as a graph called a chromatogram, where each peak corresponds to a different compound.

> **Definition:** *Carrier gas* – an inert gas that transports the sample through the GC system without reacting with it.

> **Note:** The stationary phase can be a solid (packed column) or a liquid coated on the inner wall of a narrow tube (capillary column). The choice determines the type of interactions (e.g., polarity) that are most effective for separating a given set of compounds.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a crowded hallway where people (molecules) try to walk from one end to the other. Some people stop to chat with a friend standing in the middle (the stationary phase), while others keep walking straight. The friends who stop longer cause those people to reach the door later, creating a line‑up that reflects who talked the most.

### How the pieces work together  

When the sample is injected, it instantly vaporises and merges with the carrier gas. The mixed stream enters the heated column. Inside the column, each molecule repeatedly adsorbs (sticks) to the stationary phase and then desorbs (lets go) back into the carrier gas. This “stop‑and‑go” process can be described by the equation for retention factor $k$:

$$
k = \frac{t_R - t_M}{t_M}
$$

where $t_R$ is the time a compound takes to travel through the column (retention time) and $t_M$ is the time the carrier gas alone needs (dead time). A larger $k$ means the molecule interacts more strongly with the stationary phase and stays longer.

After the column, the detector receives the exiting vapor. When a molecule reaches the detector, it produces a brief spike in the signal. The chromatogram shows these spikes as peaks; the position of each peak (its retention time) tells us which compound it is, while the height or area of the peak tells us how much of it was present.

> **Remember:** The key to good separation is choosing the right combination of carrier gas, column type, and oven temperature so that each compound has a distinct retention time.

By adjusting these parameters, chemists can separate gases, volatile liquids, and even some semi‑volatile solids after they are vaporised. GC is widely used in environmental testing (e.g., measuring pollutants in air), food safety (detecting pesticide residues), and forensic science (identifying solvents in a crime‑scene sample). The simplicity of moving a gas through a heated tube, combined with sensitive detectors, makes GC a powerful and fast tool for analysing complex mixtures.

sections.heading: Understanding Retention Time in GC
sections.body:
When a sample is injected into a gas‑chromatography (GC) instrument, the tiny amount of each component travels through a long, thin tube called the **column**. The column is packed or coated with a material that can “hold onto” (interact with) the molecules for a short time. As the carrier gas pushes the sample forward, each molecule spends a different amount of time being held and a different amount of time moving freely. The total time from injection to the moment the molecule finally leaves the column and reaches the detector is called its **retention time**.

> **Definition:** *Retention time* is the measured interval between the moment a sample is introduced into the GC and the moment a particular component exits the column and is detected.

Why does this time differ from one substance to another? Two main factors control it:

1. **Volatility** – how easily a compound turns into a gas. More volatile compounds vaporize at lower temperatures and therefore travel faster through the heated column.  
2. **Interaction with the stationary phase** – the material lining the inside of the column. Some molecules are attracted more strongly (by polarity, hydrogen‑bonding, or size) and spend more time “sticking” to the surface before they can move on.

Think of a crowded hallway where people are trying to walk from one end to the other. The hallway floor is the carrier gas flow, and the people are the molecules. Some people (highly volatile, weakly interacting) can run straight through without stopping. Others (less volatile, strongly interacting) keep bumping into obstacles (the stationary phase) and have to pause frequently, so they take longer to reach the exit. The time each person needs to get to the door is analogous to the retention time.

In a GC run, the temperature of the column is usually increased gradually (a temperature program). This helps less‑volatile compounds become more volatile as the run proceeds, shortening their retention times and allowing all components to be measured in a reasonable period.

The detector records a **peak** each time a component leaves the column. The position of the peak on the time axis is the retention time. By comparing this measured time with the retention times of known standards run under the same conditions, we can **identify** the unknown component.

> **Note:** Retention time is not an absolute property of a molecule; it depends on the column type, carrier‑gas flow rate, and temperature program. Always compare to standards run on the same instrument and settings.

### How to use retention time for identification

1. **Run a standard mixture** of compounds whose identities are known. Record each peak’s retention time; this creates a reference table.  
2. **Inject the unknown sample** under identical conditions. Measure the retention times of its peaks.  
3. **Match** each unknown peak to the closest standard retention time. If the match is within a small tolerance (often ±0.1–0.2 min), you can confidently assign the identity.

Because the same molecule will behave similarly each time the experiment is repeated (provided the conditions are unchanged), retention time acts like a molecular “fingerprint”.

### Quantitative relationship

The retention time $t_R$ can be related to the **capacity factor** $k'$ (also called the retention factor) by the equation  

$$
k' = \frac{t_R - t_M}{t_M}
$$  

where $t_M$ is the **dead time** – the time the carrier gas alone takes to travel through the column (the time of an unretained compound). A larger $k'$ means stronger interaction with the stationary phase and a longer retention time.

> **In daily life:** Think of $t_M$ as the time it takes a leaf to float down a calm river. A heavy rock (strongly retained) will sit on the riverbed much longer before it finally rolls downstream, while a light feather (highly volatile) will be carried quickly with the flow.

### Practical tips

- **Keep the column temperature stable** at the start of the run; sudden changes can shift all retention times and make comparison difficult.  
- **Use the same carrier‑gas flow rate** each time. Faster flow shortens all retention times but does not change their order.  
- **Run a blank** (no sample) to verify the dead time $t_M$ before analyzing real samples.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming a peak’s height tells you the identity. Peak height reflects concentration, not retention time. Always rely on the time axis for identification, not the size of the peak.

By understanding that retention time reflects both how readily a compound vaporizes and how strongly it interacts with the column, you can use GC as a powerful “molecular stopwatch” to separate, detect, and identify the components of complex mixtures.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Chromatography Method
sections.body:
When you have a mixture of chemicals and need to separate them, the first question is **which tool will give the clearest answer with the least hassle?**  
Two of the most common tools are Thin‑Layer Chromatography (TLC) and Gas Chromatography (GC). Both work on the same basic idea – a mixture travels through a “stationary phase” while being pushed by a “mobile phase”. The components that like the stationary phase move slowly, and the ones that like the mobile phase move quickly. By watching how far each component travels, we can tell them apart.

### How the two methods differ

| Feature | TLC (Thin‑Layer Chromatography) | GC (Gas Chromatography) |
|---------|--------------------------------|--------------------------|
| **State of the sample** | Usually a liquid or a solid that is dissolved in a solvent. | The sample must be volatile (it turns into a gas when heated). |
| **Stationary phase** | A thin layer of silica gel or alumina coated on a glass plate. | A long, thin column packed with a liquid (the “stationary liquid”) that is held inside a metal tube. |
| **Mobile phase** | A liquid solvent that climbs up the plate by capillary action. | An inert gas (often helium or nitrogen) that flows through the column. |
| **Detection** | Visual spots after the solvent front has moved; can be seen with UV light or by staining. | A detector (flame ionisation, mass spectrometer, etc.) records a signal as each component exits the column. |
| **Speed** | Minutes to an hour. | Seconds to minutes, depending on the column length and temperature program. |
| **Equipment cost** | Very low – a plate, a developing chamber, and a few solvents. | Higher – a gas chromatograph, columns, and a detector. |

> **Note:** *Volatile* means a substance that easily turns into a gas at relatively low temperatures. GC cannot analyse non‑volatile compounds unless they are chemically changed (derivatised) to become volatile.

### When to choose TLC

1. **Quick screening** – If you only need to know whether a reaction has produced the expected product, TLC can give an answer in 5–10 minutes.  
2. **Limited budget or space** – A university teaching lab often has only a few TLC plates, while a GC instrument needs electricity, gas cylinders, and regular maintenance.  
3. **Non‑volatile or thermally unstable compounds** – Large biomolecules (e.g., sugars, peptides) decompose before they could be vaporised, so TLC is the safer choice.  

**Real‑world example:** A high‑school chemistry club synthesises aspirin. After the reaction, they spot a small drop of the crude mixture on a TLC plate, develop it with a mixture of ethyl acetate and hexane, and compare the spot’s position to a pure aspirin standard. The matching spot tells them the reaction worked.

### When to choose GC

1. **Quantitative analysis** – GC’s detector gives a peak area that is proportional to the amount of each component, allowing precise measurement of concentrations.  
2. **Complex mixtures of volatile compounds** – Essential oils, environmental pollutants, and petroleum products contain many small, volatile molecules that separate well on a GC column.  
3. **High resolution** – The long column and controlled temperature program can separate compounds that differ by only a few hundredths of a Dalton in mass.  

**Real‑world example:** A food‑safety laboratory tests for pesticide residues in fruit juice. The residues are volatile enough for GC, and the instrument can detect them at parts‑per‑billion levels, providing the data needed for regulatory compliance.

### Making the decision step‑by‑step

1. **Ask yourself:** Is the sample volatile? If not, start with TLC.  
2. **Consider the goal:** Do you need a quick “yes/no” answer (TLC) or an exact concentration (GC)?  
3. **Check resources:** Do you have access to a gas chromatograph and the required gases? If not, TLC is the practical alternative.  
4. **Think about the matrix:** Complex mixtures with many similar‑looking compounds often need the higher resolving power of GC.

> **Remember:** TLC is like a quick sketch – it shows you the overall picture fast and cheaply. GC is like a high‑resolution photograph – it takes longer, costs more, but reveals fine details and exact numbers.

By matching the nature of your sample, the information you need, and the tools you have, you can choose the chromatography method that gives the best balance of speed, cost, and accuracy.

practice.q: What are the stationary phase and the mobile phase in chromatography?
practice.a: The stationary phase is the material that stays fixed in place during the separation (e.g., a thin layer of silica on a TLC plate or the inner wall of a GC column). The mobile phase is the solvent or gas that moves over or through the stationary phase, carrying the sample components with it. The different interactions of each component with these two phases cause them to travel at different speeds, leading to separation.

practice.q: In thin‑layer chromatography, why does a component that travels a short distance have a higher Rf value?
practice.a:
The Rf (retention factor) is calculated as:
Rf = (distance traveled by the component) ÷ (distance traveled by the solvent front).
If a component moves a short distance relative to the solvent front, the numerator is small, giving a low Rf value, not a higher one. Therefore, a component that travels a short distance actually has a low Rf value, indicating it interacts strongly with the stationary phase.

practice.q: Compare how polarity of the mobile phase affects separation in TLC versus GC.
practice.a: In TLC, the mobile phase is usually a liquid solvent. Increasing its polarity makes it better at dissolving polar compounds, so polar compounds spend more time in the mobile phase and move farther up the plate, giving higher Rf values. In GC, the mobile phase is an inert gas (often helium). Polarity is not a property of the gas; instead, the column’s stationary phase polarity determines separation. More polar stationary phases retain polar analytes longer, increasing their retention time. Thus, polarity adjustments are made to the liquid solvent in TLC, while in GC the column coating’s polarity is chosen to match the analytes.

practice.q: A TLC plate is developed with a solvent front that moves 8 cm. A spot for compound X moves 3 cm from the origin. Calculate the Rf for X and explain what this tells you about X’s interaction with the stationary phase.
practice.a:
Rf = distance traveled by X ÷ distance traveled by solvent front = 3 cm ÷ 8 cm = 0.375.
An Rf of 0.375 is moderate. It means compound X interacts with the stationary phase more than very non‑polar compounds (which would have higher Rf values) but less than very polar compounds (which would have low Rf values). Therefore, X has intermediate polarity relative to the chosen solvent system.

practice.q: In a gas chromatograph, two compounds, A and B, have retention times of 2.5 min and 4.0 min, respectively, under the same temperature program. Explain why B has a longer retention time and how changing the column temperature could affect both retention times.
practice.a: Retention time depends on how strongly a compound interacts with the stationary phase and its volatility. B’s longer retention time (4.0 min) indicates it either interacts more strongly with the stationary phase or is less volatile than A. If the column temperature is increased, the volatility of both compounds rises, reducing their interaction time with the stationary phase. Consequently, both retention times will decrease, but the reduction is usually larger for the less volatile compound (B), potentially narrowing the gap between A and B.

practice.q: A student must choose between TLC and GC to separate a mixture of three compounds: a non‑polar hydrocarbon, a moderately polar alcohol, and a highly polar amino acid. Which technique is more suitable for each component and why? Propose a brief experimental plan for the chosen method.
practice.a:
GC is ideal for volatile, thermally stable, and relatively non‑polar compounds. The non‑polar hydrocarbon fits GC well and will elute quickly. The moderately polar alcohol may be analyzed by GC if it can be derivatized to increase volatility; otherwise, TLC is safer. The highly polar amino acid is non‑volatile and will decompose at GC temperatures, so TLC (or another liquid‑phase method) is required.
Experimental plan:
1. Use GC with a non‑polar capillary column (e.g., 5% phenyl‑methylpolysiloxane) to analyze the hydrocarbon. Set the oven temperature to start low (e.g., 50 °C) and ramp to 200 °C to ensure elution.
2. Prepare a TLC plate coated with silica gel (polar stationary phase). Develop it with a solvent system of moderate polarity (e.g., ethyl acetate : hexane = 1:1). Spot the mixture; the hydrocarbon will have a high Rf, the alcohol a medium Rf, and the amino acid a low Rf (or may require a more polar solvent). Visualize with UV light or ninhydrin spray for the amino acid. This combined approach separates each component using the method best suited to its chemical nature.

data.recap: Chromatography separates the components of a mixture by moving it through a stationary phase while a mobile phase carries it along. Molecules that interact strongly with the stationary phase move slower, creating distinct zones that can be identified. Thin‑layer chromatography (TLC) uses a flat plate and a liquid mobile phase, while gas chromatography (GC) uses a heated column and a gaseous mobile phase. Retention factor (Rf) in TLC and retention time in GC are numerical ways to compare how far or how long each component travels.
